name: Kepkiriwát
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Extinct Tupian; only Rondon & Faria 1948 wordlist (10pp); no phonological description.

sources.citation: Nikulin, Andrey & Rafael Andrade. 2020. The rise and fall of approximants in the Tuparian languages. Journal of Language Relationship 18(3-4): 284-319. doi:10.31826/jlr-2020-183-412.
sources.note: Kepkiriwát is not among the languages analysed (Wayoró, Tuparí, Mekéns, Akuntsú, Makurap); it appears only in the reference list via Lévi-Strauss's unpublished ms 'Vocabulaires de trois langues: Kabišiana, Kepkiri-uat et de São Pedro'. For the branch it notes contrastive stress in Tuparí and Akuntsú and tone in Makurap, and flags Proto-Tuparian prosody as unreconstructed. Silent on Kepkiriwát stress.

sources.citation: Aragon, Carolina Coelho. 2014. A grammar of Akuntsú, a Tupían language. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa. (text already held by the project)
sources.note: Mentions Kepkiriwát only historically: Rondon recorded 117 words in 1913 on the Barão de Melgaço river and Barbosa de Faria a larger list in 1927 (Rondon & Faria 1948); nothing on Kepkiriwát phonology.

sources.citation: Galucio, Ana Vilacy & Antônia Fernanda Nogueira. 2012 [2011]. Comparative study of the Tupari branch of the Tupi family: contributions to understanding its historical development and internal classification. In: Memorias del V Congreso de Idiomas Indígenas de Latinoamérica (CILLA V), Austin: AILLA.
sources.note: Standard Proto-Tuparí comparison; would confirm whether any modern Tuparí-branch comparative work uses or comments on the Kepkiriwát data (Nikulin & Andrade 2020 do not). AILLA server is behind an anti-bot wall (Anubis) and could not be downloaded.

sources.citation: Loukotka, Čestmír. 1949. Sur quelques langues inconnues de l'Amérique du Sud. Lingua Posnaniensis 1: 53-82. [§13 'Kepkeriwat', pp.76-78: wordlists from Joaquim Gondim's 1924 ms (Manaus SPI archive, copied by Nimuendajú) and an anonymous SPI ms ('Quepiqueriuate')]
sources.note: Nothing; bare comparative wordlist (c. 45 items) with accent marks on some forms but no comment on accent or pronunciation.

sources.citation: Rondon, Cândido M. S. & João Barbosa de Faria. 1948. Glossário geral das tribos silvícolas de Mato-Grosso e outras da Amazônia e do Norte do Brasil, Tomo I. (Conselho Nacional de Proteção aos Índios / Comissão Rondon, Publicação n. 76, Anexo 5 – Etnografia.) Rio de Janeiro: Imprensa Nacional. 257 pp. [Kepkiriwát = 'Quêpi-quiri-uáte': comparative Glossário n.2 pp.117-162; Rondon's May-1913 list pp.177-182; Barbosa de Faria's Jan-1927 list pp.185-192; 'Convenções adotadas' pp.10-11]
sources.note: Only a transcription convention (p.11, item IV): diacritics placed on vowels in the vocabularies — the example given is Kepkiriwát oquĕt 'filho/filha' — mark 'the strong and long sounds of tonic syllables'; footnote says the sign is a small upward-open semicircle that the printers omitted in some vocabularies. The Kepkiriwát lists themselves (pp.177-192) carry per-word acute/circumflex/breve marks (e.g. popé, tacá, amixá, iniamú, dorú; but also Uóque, Ócüpe, Japiquite) with no statement of a positional rule and no phonological notes.

sources.citation: Nikulin, Andrey & Fernando O. de Carvalho. 2022. A revised reconstruction of the Proto-Tupian vowel system. Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi. Ciências Humanas 17(2): e20210035, 40 pp. doi:10.1590/2178-2547-BGOELDI-2021-0035.
sources.venue: Boletim do Museu Paraense Emílio Goeldi

tone.quote: Data quoted from premodern sources, which are not expected to faithfully represent all the relevant phonological oppositions, are given ‘verbatim’ enclosed in chevrons. [...] The default reflex of PT *ə in Kepkiriwat appears to be o rather than e, as in ‹uóque›R, ‹uóc›B ‘house, village’, ‹óp›B ‘leaf’, ‹gó›B ‘cultivated field’ (Rondon & Faria, 1948, pp. 181, 187, 191) < PT *ək ‘house’ or maybe the first person form *o-jək ‘my house’, *jəp ‘leaf’, *ŋgə ‘cultivated field’. This suggests that Kepkiriwat is not a Tuparian language but rather forms a branch of its own. The issue awaits further investigation.
tone.locator: p. 4, notational conventions at the end of the Introduction; and fn. 21 on p. 21, section on the Tuparian reflexes of PT *ə
